set.stem: An 82-year-old woman is admitted for observation after presenting with dizziness, and the rhythm strip shown is recorded on the monitor. She has no history of cardiac disease, diabetes or hypertension. On questioning she reports several previous episodes of transient dizziness and one brief syncope. Examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the best plan of care?
options: Reassurance; this is a benign condition and needs no treatment
Reassurance and advice not to drive until symptom-free; no other treatment
Nuclear cardiac stress testing, with treatment depending on the result
set.explanation: The strip shows a burst of rapid irregular supraventricular tachycardia that stops abruptly and is followed by a long pause before slow beats resume – the tachycardia–bradycardia form of sick sinus syndrome. Symptomatic pauses (dizziness, syncope) are a class I indication for permanent pacing, which also allows rate-controlling or antiarrhythmic drugs to be used safely for the tachycardia. If the tachycardia is AF she also needs anticoagulation (CHA2DS2-VASc at least 3), not aspirin; reassurance alone is unsafe, and ischaemia testing does not treat conduction disease.

why: Same idea as arr-0043 (benign atrial/ventricular ectopics in a structurally normal heart: reassurance)

set.stem: An active 78-year-old woman with hypertension presents with a new left hemiparesis; CT excludes haemorrhage, and cardiac monitoring shows atrial fibrillation. She was in sinus rhythm at a check-up 3 months earlier. Optimal management at discharge includes review of her antihypertensive therapy, a ventricular rate-control agent and which of the following?
options: An implantable cardioverter-defibrillator/permanent pacemaker to avoid the need for anticoagulation
Antiplatelet therapy such as aspirin, without anticoagulation
Antiplatelet therapy plus warfarin with a target INR of 1.5
Long-term oral anticoagulation (a DOAC, or warfarin with a target INR of 2.0–3.0)
set.explanation: Ischaemic stroke with AF gives a CHA2DS2-VASc score of at least 6 (stroke 2, age 75 or over 2, hypertension 1, female 1), so lifelong oral anticoagulation is indicated – a DOAC is preferred, or warfarin with a target INR of 2.0–3.0 (2.5–3.5 is reserved for some mechanical valves). It is started within days of the stroke, earlier for small infarcts and later for large ones. Aspirin alone is far less effective, adding aspirin to anticoagulation increases bleeding without benefit, and an INR of 1.5 is subtherapeutic. An ICD or pacemaker does not prevent thromboembolism, and cardioversion does not remove the need for anticoagulation.

why: Anticoagulation option updated to include DOACs (now preferred); key unchanged

set.stem: A 72-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension develops a viral upper respiratory infection. On the second day he has palpitations and attends the emergency department. His BP is 118/78 mmHg and he is otherwise well. The rhythm strip (lead V1) is shown. What is the best next step in management?
set.explanation: The V1 strip shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at about 130/min with discrete atrial (flutter) waves at about 250/min, two for every QRS – atrial flutter with 2:1 block. He is haemodynamically stable, so the first step is ventricular rate control with an AV-nodal blocker such as IV metoprolol (or diltiazem), followed by assessment for anticoagulation and elective cardioversion or ablation. Adenosine only transiently increases the block (useful diagnostically) and does not treat flutter, amiodarone is a second-line drug, emergency cardioversion is for adverse features, and chest compressions are for cardiac arrest.

set.stem: An asymptomatic 65-year-old man with diabetes attends the emergency department with a sports-related right shoulder injury. His pulse is irregular, and the rhythm strip shown is recorded; BP and the rest of the examination are normal. What is the best immediate management?
set.explanation: The strip shows the PR interval lengthening from beat to beat until a P wave is not conducted, after which the cycle restarts with a short PR – Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) second-degree AV block. The block lies in the AV node, rarely progresses and, in an asymptomatic patient, needs only observation, review of AV-nodal blocking drugs (beta-blockers, rate-limiting calcium-channel blockers, digoxin) and ECG follow-up. Atropine or isoprenaline is for symptomatic bradycardia, pacing for symptomatic or infranodal block, and cardioversion has no role.

set.stem: In the intensive care unit, a monitored patient suddenly becomes unresponsive and pulseless, and the monitor shows ventricular tachycardia. A defibrillator is immediately available. What is the best first treatment?
set.explanation: Pulseless VT is managed exactly like ventricular fibrillation: in a monitored, witnessed arrest with a defibrillator at hand, give an immediate unsynchronised shock (biphasic 120–200 J; up to three successive shocks may be given in this setting), then resume CPR. Synchronised cardioversion is for VT with a pulse – in pulseless VT, attempting to synchronise only delays the shock. Adrenaline 1 mg is given after the third shock and then every 3–5 minutes, with amiodarone 300 mg (or lidocaine) after the third shock.

why: The two defibrillation-energy options (200 J vs 360 J) were not a valid discriminator; replaced by unsynchronised defibrillation vs synchronised cardioversion, and the cardiac-arrest amiodarone dose corrected to 300 mg
Same idea as arr-0064 (stable narrow-complex tachycardia after failed vagal manoeuvres: IV adenosine)

set.stem: A patient has been on the coronary care unit for 24 hours with an acute anterior myocardial infarction. He develops the rhythm shown, although his BP remains stable at 110/68 mmHg. What is the best next step in management?
options: Pacing (temporary transvenous, then assessment for a permanent pacemaker)
set.explanation: The strip shows P waves at a regular rate marching through slower, regular QRS complexes with no fixed relationship – complete (third-degree) heart block. After an anterior MI this reflects extensive septal necrosis with infranodal block; the ventricular escape rhythm is slow and unreliable and can fail abruptly, so pacing is indicated even when BP is maintained. Digoxin and propranolol would worsen AV conduction, lidocaine can suppress the escape rhythm, and cardioversion is for tachyarrhythmias.

set.stem: A 62-year-old man with COPD develops a viral upper respiratory infection and starts an over-the-counter decongestant. Shortly afterwards he has palpitations and attends the emergency department, where the rhythm strip shown is recorded. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: The baseline shows continuous regular sawtooth flutter waves at about 300/min, with a QRS after every fourth wave giving a regular ventricular rate of about 75/min – atrial flutter with 4:1 AV block. Sympathomimetic decongestants (pseudoephedrine) and underlying lung disease are recognised triggers. Atrial tachycardia with block shows discrete P waves separated by an isoelectric baseline (classically digoxin toxicity), a junctional rhythm has absent or retrograde P waves, and AF produces an irregular rhythm without organised atrial activity.

why: Replaced the self-contradictory distractor 'complete heart block with 2:1 block' with atrial fibrillation; paroxysmal atrial tachycardia renamed atrial tachycardia

set.stem: An 80-year-old woman is admitted with dizziness. Monitoring shows atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response, which is controlled with a beta-blocker. Echocardiography shows an enlarged left atrium, an ejection fraction of 50% and no diastolic dysfunction. She is now asymptomatic, with BP 130/80 mmHg and an irregularly irregular pulse of about 80/min. What is the best management strategy for her arrhythmia?
set.explanation: In an older patient whose AF is now rate-controlled and asymptomatic, continued rate control with long-term anticoagulation is the preferred strategy: a dilated left atrium predicts early recurrence after cardioversion, and rhythm control has not improved survival in older patients with established AF. Her CHA2DS2-VASc score is at least 3 (age 75 or over, female), so oral anticoagulation (preferably a DOAC) is indicated whatever strategy is chosen; cardioversion without anticoagulation, electrical or chemical, would be dangerous. Rhythm control is reserved for patients who remain symptomatic despite adequate rate control, and early rhythm control is considered mainly in recently diagnosed AF.

set.stem: During medical screening of new military recruits, an 18-year-old man reports several episodes of palpitations and syncope over the past few years. Examination is unremarkable. Excerpts from his ECG are shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Previous myocardial infarction secondary to coronary artery disease
set.explanation: The tracings show a short PR interval with a slurred upstroke of the QRS (delta wave) and a widened QRS – ventricular pre-excitation through an accessory pathway, which with tachyarrhythmias constitutes Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome. Negative delta waves can mimic the pathological Q waves of an old MI; long QT syndrome shows a prolonged QTc with a normal PR, HCM shows LVH voltage with deep narrow septal Q waves, and mitral stenosis gives P mitrale or AF. Syncope with pre-excitation warrants an electrophysiology study and catheter ablation of the pathway.

set.stem: A 38-year-old man with no past medical history is referred after an abnormal preoperative ECG, and long QT syndrome is confirmed on repeat ECGs. His father had a heart condition diagnosed in his 20s, and he himself has had episodes of syncope after exertion. He is started on a beta-blocker and an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator is planned. Loss of function of which of the following is most commonly associated with his condition?
set.explanation: Congenital long QT syndrome is most often caused by loss-of-function mutations in cardiac potassium channels – KCNQ1 (IKs, LQT1, events triggered by exercise and swimming) and KCNH2/hERG (IKr, LQT2, triggered by sudden noise or emotion) – which delay ventricular repolarisation and predispose to torsades de pointes. LQT3 is a gain (not loss) of function of the SCN5A sodium channel, whereas loss of sodium-channel function causes Brugada syndrome; SA and AV node disease alter rate and PR, not QT. Management is a beta-blocker (nadolol or propranolol), avoidance of QT-prolonging drugs and hypokalaemia, and an ICD for survivors of arrest or recurrent syncope despite treatment.

set.stem: A 55-year-old man with ischaemic heart disease presents with palpitations for the past 10 days. His pulse is 130/min and irregularly irregular. He had one previous episode of atrial fibrillation 3 months ago, which was terminated by elective cardioversion after anticoagulation with warfarin. Which term best describes his arrhythmia?
set.explanation: AF is classified by its time course: paroxysmal AF terminates spontaneously or with intervention within 7 days; persistent AF lasts more than 7 days (including episodes terminated by cardioversion after that time); long-standing persistent lasts more than a year while rhythm control is still pursued; and permanent AF is accepted by patient and doctor with no further attempts at rhythm control. His current episode has lasted 10 days and his previous episode needed elective cardioversion, so this is persistent AF. Atrial flutter gives a regular rhythm, and secondary AF is AF with an acute reversible trigger such as surgery or thyrotoxicosis.

set.stem: A 72-year-old man with hypertension and ischaemic heart disease presents with light-headedness. He takes bisoprolol, amlodipine and aspirin. Heart rate is 38/min, BP 96/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on air and temperature 37.1 °C. The ECG shows regular P–P and R–R intervals with no relationship between the P waves and the QRS complexes. What would you expect to hear on auscultation of the heart?
set.explanation: Regular P waves and regular QRS complexes with no relationship between them is complete heart block. Because the interval between atrial and ventricular contraction varies from beat to beat, the mitral and tricuspid leaflets are in different positions when ventricular systole begins, so the intensity of S1 varies (and intermittent cannon a waves appear in the JVP). A loud S1 occurs with mitral stenosis or a short PR, a soft S1 with a long PR or mitral regurgitation, a loud S2 with systemic or pulmonary hypertension, and a soft S2 with severe aortic stenosis. He needs his bisoprolol stopped and pacing.

set.stem: A 56-year-old man is brought in by paramedics after fainting this morning; he is now conscious but pale and light-headed, with no injuries. His heart rate is 37/min, respiratory rate 16/min and BP 105/70 mmHg. The ECG shows sinus bradycardia with a prolonged PR interval. What is the initial management?
set.explanation: Bradycardia with an adverse feature – here syncope; the others are shock, myocardial ischaemia and heart failure – is treated first with IV atropine 500 micrograms, repeated every 3–5 minutes to a maximum of 3 mg. If there is no response, or there is a risk of asystole (Mobitz II, complete block with a broad QRS, recent asystole, pauses over 3 seconds), move to transcutaneous pacing or an isoprenaline or adrenaline infusion as a bridge to transvenous pacing. Adenosine is for regular narrow-complex tachycardia and would worsen the bradycardia, atropine is not given orally in this setting, and IM adrenaline is for anaphylaxis.

why: Removed 'has not regained consciousness' (an unresponsive patient would need an ABC/arrest assessment rather than simply atropine); the patient is now conscious after syncope

set.stem: A 75-year-old woman is admitted to the acute medical unit with pneumonia. Her only past history is a transient ischaemic attack 2 months ago. On admission the ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 103/min. She is treated with IV fluids and antibiotics and improves; two further ECGs overnight show sinus rhythm, and next day she is medically fit for discharge. What is the single most appropriate management of her atrial fibrillation?
set.explanation: Her CHA2DS2-VASc score is 5 (age 75 or over 2, female 1, previous TIA 2), so oral anticoagulation, preferably a DOAC, is indicated. AF that is paroxysmal or first appears during an acute illness such as pneumonia commonly recurs and carries a real stroke risk, and the decision to anticoagulate depends on stroke risk, not on whether sinus rhythm has returned. Aspirin is not recommended for stroke prevention in AF, and waiting for a Holter recording or a repeat ECG only delays protection; bleeding risk is assessed to correct modifiable factors, not to withhold treatment.

set.stem: A 30-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with sudden-onset palpitations. BP is 124/84 mmHg and pulse 150/min. The ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia. Vagal manoeuvres fail, IV access is obtained and adenosine 6 mg is given with no effect. What is the most appropriate next step?
set.explanation: For a stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia that persists after vagal manoeuvres, adenosine is given as a rapid IV bolus with a flush: 6 mg first, then 12 mg if unsuccessful, then 18 mg (Resuscitation Council UK). Repeating 6 mg is unlikely to work; verapamil is the alternative when adenosine is contraindicated or fails; synchronised cardioversion is for adverse features or drug failure; and catheter ablation is the definitive treatment for recurrent SVT rather than the acute step.

set.stem: Each of the following may cause left bundle branch block EXCEPT:
set.explanation: LBBB reflects disease of the left-sided conducting system and is seen with ischaemic heart disease, hypertension and LVH, aortic stenosis, cardiomyopathies and idiopathic degenerative fibrosis of the conducting system (Lenègre–Lev disease). An ostium secundum atrial septal defect causes right ventricular volume overload and characteristically gives incomplete or complete right bundle branch block with right axis deviation, whereas left axis deviation suggests an ostium primum defect.

set.stem: A 35-year-old man presents to the emergency department after an episode of syncope. The ECG shows sinus rhythm at 85/min, QRS duration 110 ms, PR interval 180 ms and corrected QT interval 500 ms. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the ECG abnormality?
set.explanation: A QTc of 500 ms is prolonged (normal under about 450 ms in men and 460 ms in women; above 500 ms carries a high risk of torsades de pointes). Hypokalaemia is a common cause, with flattened T waves and prominent U waves; hypomagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia, many drugs (macrolides, antipsychotics, methadone, class Ia and III antiarrhythmics) and congenital channelopathies are others. Hypercalcaemia and digoxin shorten the QT interval, hyperkalaemia causes peaked T waves without QT prolongation, and fever does not prolong the QT.

why: Replaced two debatable distractors (cyclizine; subdural haemorrhage – intracranial bleeding can prolong the QT) with causes that do not prolong the QT

set.stem: A 34-year-old woman is admitted after a collapse, and the ECG shows polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. Which one of the following is NOT associated with an increased risk of torsades de pointes?
set.explanation: Torsades de pointes occurs on a background of QT prolongation: tricyclic antidepressants (and many other drugs), subarachnoid haemorrhage, hypothermia and congenital long QT syndromes such as Romano–Ward (autosomal dominant, normal hearing) and Jervell and Lange-Nielsen (recessive, with deafness) all prolong the QT interval. Hypercalcaemia shortens the QT; it is hypocalcaemia, together with hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia, that predisposes to torsades. Acute treatment is IV magnesium sulfate 2 g, correction of electrolytes and withdrawal of offending drugs.

set.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with a 4-day history of palpitations and increasing breathlessness on exertion. The ECG shows atrial fibrillation at 118/min. He has brittle asthma, hypertension and heart failure, and a recent echocardiogram showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 32%. What is the most appropriate drug to control his heart rate?
topics: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
set.explanation: In AF with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction, rate-limiting calcium-channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem) are contraindicated because they are negatively inotropic, and a beta-blocker – the usual first choice – is precluded by his brittle asthma (sotalol is also a non-selective beta-blocker). Digoxin slows AV-nodal conduction without depressing contractility and is the appropriate rate-control drug here. Amiodarone can slow the rate acutely in heart failure but is a rhythm-control drug with substantial long-term toxicity, kept for when other options fail.

set.stem: A 72-year-old man presents with lethargy and palpitations for the past 4–5 days. His pulse is 123/min and irregularly irregular, BP 118/70 mmHg, and his chest is clear. An ECG confirms atrial fibrillation. What is the most appropriate drug to control his heart rate?
set.explanation: For stable AF without heart failure, first-line rate control is a beta-blocker such as bisoprolol or a rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker (diltiazem or verapamil), aiming initially for a resting rate below 110/min. Digoxin monotherapy is reserved for sedentary patients or when other agents are contraindicated, because it controls the rate poorly on exertion. Amiodarone and flecainide are rhythm-control drugs, and amlodipine is a dihydropyridine that does not slow AV-nodal conduction. He also needs CHA2DS2-VASc assessment for anticoagulation.

set.stem: Which one of the following is NOT an indication for insertion of a temporary pacemaker?
options: Complete heart block after an inferior MI, with normal blood pressure
Complete heart block after an anterior MI, with normal blood pressure
Bradycardia-dependent torsades de pointes recurring despite IV magnesium
Mobitz type II heart block after an anterior MI, with normal blood pressure
Symptomatic bradycardia not responding to drug treatment
set.explanation: Complete heart block after an inferior MI is usually due to AV-nodal ischaemia (right coronary artery), has a narrow-complex junctional escape at 40–60/min, often responds to atropine and generally resolves within days of reperfusion, so a haemodynamically stable patient does not need temporary pacing. Complete heart block or Mobitz II after an anterior MI implies extensive infranodal septal damage with an unreliable broad-complex escape, so temporary pacing is indicated even with a normal BP. Temporary pacing is also used for symptomatic bradycardia refractory to drugs and for overdrive pacing of bradycardia-dependent torsades de pointes.

why: Replaced 'trifascicular block prior to surgery' (asymptomatic bifascicular block with first-degree AV block no longer warrants prophylactic temporary pacing, making it a second correct answer) with a clear indication
